thoughts: Spanish a is a consistent open vowel, unlike the several sounds English a can represent.
description: Say “ah,” as in the first sound of “father.” Keep it short and clear; don’t turn it into the “ay” sound in “day.”

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar Spanish word for friend

thoughts: Spanish b has a familiar English-like pronunciation at the start of an utterance and a softer pronunciation between vowels.
description: At the start of an utterance or after m or n, pronounce b much like English b in “boy.” Between vowels, keep your lips close but do not press them fully together, making a softer b-like sound.

example_words.cultural_context: A word often seen on food packaging

thoughts: The standalone c is illustrated before a, o, or u; ce, ci, and ch have separate guides.
description: Pronounce c like the English k in “key” before a, o, or u.

example_words.cultural_context: Common Spanish word for a house

thoughts: Spanish d has a firm sound at the start of a word and a softer sound between vowels. Word-final d has a separate guide.
description: At the start of a word, d sounds much like English d, but the tongue touches the upper teeth. Between vowels, it softens: let air pass gently between the tongue and upper teeth, a little like the th in “this.”

example_words.cultural_context: A Spanish word sometimes used in English

thoughts: Spanish e has one steady vowel sound; unlike English, it does not glide toward an “ee” sound.
description: Say the vowel in English “bed,” but keep it steady and crisp. Do not turn it into the sound of “ay.”

thoughts: Spanish f has the same sound as English f in “fan.”
description: Pronounce it like the f in English “fan”: touch your upper teeth to your lower lip and blow air through.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar word from coffee shops
Sounds much like the English word “photo”

thoughts: The standalone g represents a hard g sound, which often softens between vowels. The combinations ge, gi, gue, and gui have separate guides.
description: Usually like the g in English “go.” Between vowels, it is often softer: keep your tongue close to the roof of your mouth without fully stopping the airflow.

example_words.cultural_context: A common word for a familiar animal
The well-known dance and music style
A Spanish word many English speakers recognize

thoughts: The letter h is silent in these examples. Its spelling does not add a sound.
description: Do not pronounce h, even at the beginning of a word. For example, hola starts with an o sound, not the English h sound in “hello.”

example_words.cultural_context: Same meaning as the English word
Same meaning as the English word

thoughts: The letter i usually represents a clear, short-duration /i/ sound. Choose examples where it is pronounced as a vowel, rather than as part of a guided spelling combination.
description: Pronounce i like the “ee” in “see,” but keep it crisp and avoid sliding into another sound.

example_words.cultural_context: A useful word for an island or vacation destination
The same name for the well-known Japanese food

thoughts: Spanish j usually sounds like a strong English h, not the j in “job.” Its exact strength varies by region.
description: Make a breathy sound like the h in “hat,” often with a little more friction farther back in your throat. Do not pronounce it like the j in “job.”

thoughts: Spanish k represents the same basic sound as English k. It is uncommon in native Spanish words but appears in familiar loanwords.
description: Pronounce k as in English “kite”: briefly stop the air at the back of your mouth, then release it.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar metric unit of weight

thoughts: Spanish single l is a clear l sound, including at the end of a word. The separate spelling ll has its own guide.
description: Make an l sound with the tip of your tongue touching the ridge behind your upper teeth. It resembles the l in English “leaf,” but stays clear rather than becoming the darker l many English speakers use in “full.”

example_words.cultural_context: Familiar from names and words related to the moon
A common Spanish word for the sun

thoughts: Spanish m is the same familiar consonant sound as English m.
description: Pronounce m as in English “mom”: close your lips and let the sound come through your nose.

thoughts: Spanish n is usually familiar to English speakers. Before some consonants, its tongue position may shift naturally, but these examples teach the straightforward n sound.
description: Pronounce n like the n in English “no”: touch your tongue just behind your upper front teeth and let the sound pass through your nose. Keep it distinct from Spanish ñ.

thoughts: The letter ñ consistently represents one sound, similar to the middle sound in English “canyon.”
description: Pronounce ñ like the “ny” in “canyon”: make one blended sound, not a separate n followed by a separate y.

example_words.cultural_context: Weather pattern mentioned in the news

thoughts: Spanish o is a steady vowel, unlike the English long o, which often glides toward an oo sound.
description: Say a short, steady “oh,” with rounded lips. Don’t add the “oo” glide heard at the end of English “go.”

example_words.cultural_context: Looks and means much like the English word

thoughts: Spanish p is the familiar /p/ sound, but it usually has less of the puff of air heard at the start of English words like “pie.”
description: Press your lips together, then release them for a crisp p sound. Keep the release light, without a strong puff of air.

example_words.cultural_context: The familiar food; Spanish speakers pronounce its p with a light release.

thoughts: In ordinary Spanish words, q occurs in que and qui, which have their own guides. There is no separate q sound to demonstrate here.
description: The letter q does not have a sound on its own in ordinary Spanish words. It appears with u in que and qui; consult those guides for their pronunciation.

thoughts: This guide focuses on single r within a word. Word-initial r, word-final r, and rr have separate guides.
description: Within a word, a single r is usually a quick tap of the tongue against the ridge just behind your upper teeth. It sounds like the quick middle sound in many American pronunciations of “butter,” not the English r in “red.”

example_words.cultural_context: Familiar food used for tacos and wraps

thoughts: Spanish s is usually the same sound as the s in English 'see.' In some Latin American accents, an s at the end of a syllable may sound like a soft h or disappear, but these examples use the clear s sound.
description: Pronounce s like the s in English 'see': a crisp, voiceless hiss. Unlike the s in English 'rose,' it does not sound like z.

thoughts: Spanish t is familiar to English speakers, though its tongue placement and lack of a strong puff of air may take a little practice.
description: Like the t in English “stop,” but place the tip of your tongue against your upper front teeth and release it without a strong puff of air.

example_words.cultural_context: Same word in English for an outdoor seating area
A common food with a similar English name

thoughts: The letter u usually represents a clear /u/ sound, similar to the vowel in English “too.” Avoid examples where u is silent or belongs to a separately taught spelling combination.
description: Say “oo” as in “too,” but keep your lips rounded and the vowel short and steady.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar Spanish number and card-game name
Familiar from names and the word “lunar”

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, v is pronounced like b, not English v. Its pronunciation changes slightly with its surroundings.
description: Pronounce v like Spanish b: after a pause, close both lips as for English b. Between vowels, bring the lips close together without fully closing them. Do not touch your upper teeth to your lower lip as you would for English v.

example_words.cultural_context: A common word on restaurant menus
Familiar from the holiday greeting “Feliz Navidad”

thoughts: In common Spanish loanwords, w usually has the same sound as English w. Pronunciation can vary in some borrowed words, so these examples use the w sound.
description: Pronounce w as in English “web”: round your lips briefly, then move into the next vowel.

thoughts: Spanish x usually sounds like the x in English “taxi,” but its pronunciation varies in some words and names.
description: Usually say “ks,” as in English “taxi.” In México, x instead sounds like a stronger English “h.” At the start of xilófono, it sounds like “s.”

example_words.cultural_context: The same everyday vehicle as in English
The familiar country name; here x has a different sound
The familiar musical instrument; here x sounds like s

thoughts: This guide covers consonant y, not word-final y or combinations such as ay and oy, which have separate guides.
description: Usually like the y in English “yes,” but often with a slightly firmer, buzzier sound. In some Latin American accents, it sounds closer to the j in “jam.”

example_words.cultural_context: A basic word for talking about yourself
Name of the well-known Mesoamerican civilization
A common word on beach and travel signs

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, z is pronounced like s, not like the English z. The examples avoid za, zo, and zu, which have separate guides.
description: Pronounce z like the s in “see,” with no vocal-cord vibration. It is not the buzzing z in English “zoo.”

example_words.cultural_context: Often heard in the greeting “Feliz Navidad”

thoughts: Á has the same vowel sound as a; the accent mark shows that its syllable is stressed.
description: Say “ah,” like the vowel in “father,” with a clear, steady sound. Stress the syllable containing á.

thoughts: The accent marks the e as stressed; it does not give it a different vowel sound.
description: Pronounce é like Spanish e: roughly the vowel in “bed,” but a little tenser. Keep it short and steady, without turning it into “ay.” The accent tells you to stress that syllable.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar word from coffee shops

thoughts: The accent marks this vowel as stressed. English speakers already know the vowel sound, but should keep it short and steady rather than turning it into a glide.
description: Pronounce í like the “ee” in “see,” with stress on that syllable. Keep the vowel pure, without an extra sound at the end.

example_words.cultural_context: A basic Spanish word for yes
A common word used in greetings such as buenos días
A word seen in Latin American food names

thoughts: The accent marks stress; ó has the same vowel sound as Spanish o.
description: Pronounce ó as a clear, stressed “oh.” Keep the vowel steady rather than gliding toward “oo” as English “oh” often does.

thoughts: The accent marks a stressed vowel; it does not change the basic sound of u.
description: Pronounce ú like the “oo” in “food,” with your lips rounded. Give that syllable the stress.

example_words.cultural_context: South American country famous for Machu Picchu
The list of food and drinks at a restaurant
A familiar word for songs and instrumental sounds

thoughts: In standard Spanish, ü appears in güe and güi. The dots show that the u is pronounced, rather than silent. These larger spellings have separate guides, so this entry focuses only on the sound of ü.
description: Pronounce ü like the English “w” in “we”: a quick glide, not a full “oo” vowel. It makes the u audible in spellings such as güe and güi.

example_words.cultural_context: Describes someone who speaks two languages
A common word for feeling embarrassed

thoughts: Spanish ch has the same sound as English ch in “cheese.”
description: Pronounce ch like the ch in English “cheese,” not like the sh in “chef.”

example_words.cultural_context: A pepper used in spicy food

thoughts: In most of Latin America, ll has the same sound as consonant y. Some regions pronounce it more like English sh or zh.
description: Usually pronounce ll like the y in “yes,” not like two English l’s. Regional pronunciations vary.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar food name in English
Often seen on Mexican restaurant menus

thoughts: In standard Latin American Spanish, rr represents a rolled r, distinct from the single tap often made by r between vowels.
description: Roll the tip of your tongue against the ridge just behind your upper teeth, letting it vibrate briefly. Unlike the English r, the tongue tip makes repeated contact.

example_words.cultural_context: The Spanish word for a familiar musical instrument

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, ce is pronounced /se/, not like English “che.”
description: Say “seh”: an English s sound followed by a short, clear e, like the vowel in “met.”

example_words.cultural_context: Common word for a town or city center
A word often seen on restaurant menus

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, ci uses the familiar English /s/ sound followed by an /i/ vowel.
description: Say “see”: c sounds like English s, and i sounds like “ee.” Do not pronounce c like k.

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, ge has the same initial consonant sound as Spanish j, followed by the vowel e. It never sounds like the English g in “gem.”
description: Say a breathy h, as in English “hello,” followed by a short eh sound. In some regions, the h-like sound is raspier, made farther back in the throat.

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, gi begins with the same sound as Spanish j, followed by the vowel i. It does not have the English g sound in “gift.”
description: Pronounce gi like a breathy English h followed by “ee”: roughly “hee.”

example_words.cultural_context: Similar in meaning and spelling to “giant”
Same meaning as the English word

thoughts: The u is silent in gue; it keeps g hard before e. The pronounced sounds are familiar to English speakers.
description: Pronounce gue like “geh,” with the hard g in “get.” Do not pronounce the u. For a pronounced u, Spanish uses güe.

example_words.cultural_context: A well-known Latin dance and music style

thoughts: The u is silent in gui; the spelling keeps g hard before i. Use examples with an unaccented i and no ü.
description: Pronounce gui like “gee” in “geese”: a hard g followed by an ee sound. Do not pronounce the u.

example_words.cultural_context: The Spanish word for the familiar musical instrument
A common verb used for following someone or continuing
The bird of prey often seen on flags and emblems

thoughts: The dots over ü mean the u is pronounced; without them, the u in gue is silent.
description: Say it roughly like “gweh”: a g sound followed by a quick English w sound and Spanish e, similar to the e in “bed.”

example_words.cultural_context: The bird traditionally said to deliver babies
An everyday word for feeling embarrassed
Describes someone who speaks two languages

thoughts: The diaeresis makes the u audible; without it, gui has a silent u.
description: Say “gwee,” like the start of English “Gwen” followed by “ee.” The g is hard, as in “go,” and the ü is pronounced like a quick English w.

example_words.cultural_context: An affectionate way to refer to water
A scraping instrument heard in Latin American music

thoughts: The u is silent in que; the letters make the familiar English sound /ke/.
description: Pronounce que like “keh”: a k sound followed by the e sound in “bed.” Do not pronounce the u.

example_words.cultural_context: A common word for a public park

thoughts: In Spanish, the u in qui is silent; the spelling represents the familiar sounds k + ee.
description: Say “kee,” as in the start of English “key.” Do not pronounce the u.

example_words.cultural_context: The same insect as in English
The age celebrated at a quinceañera

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, z before a sounds like s, not English z. The a is a clear 'ah' sound.
description: Pronounce za like 'sah': an s sound followed by 'ah,' as in 'father.' Do not use the buzzing z sound in English 'zebra.'

example_words.cultural_context: Familiar word for a town square or shopping area
Common word seen on restaurant and bar menus

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, z sounds like English s, not English z. The o is a short, pure vowel without the glide often heard in English “go.”
description: Pronounce zo roughly like “soh,” with an unvoiced s sound and a steady o vowel. Do not use the buzzing z sound in English “zoo.”

example_words.cultural_context: Name of the masked fictional hero
Often heard in the expression un abrazo

thoughts: In Latin American Spanish, z sounds like English s, not English z. The u has the vowel sound in “too.”
description: Pronounce zu like “soo,” with an s sound at the start—not the z sound in English “zoo.”

example_words.cultural_context: An everyday word for a left-handed person
The sound a bee or mosquito makes

thoughts: At the beginning of a word, Spanish r is pronounced with a trill, not like the usual English r.
description: Tap the tip of your tongue rapidly against the ridge behind your upper teeth, making it vibrate. This is the rolled r; avoid the usual English r sound.

example_words.cultural_context: The same word as in English.
The name for a familiar alcoholic drink.

thoughts: At the end of a word, Spanish r is usually a brief tongue-tip tap, not the sustained English r.
description: Tap the tip of your tongue quickly against the ridge just behind your upper teeth. Keep it brief; do not curl your tongue back as you might for an English final r.

example_words.cultural_context: A Spanish form of address often heard in movies and TV
A familiar word from Spanish songs and phrases
Appears in Spanish place names such as Viña del Mar

thoughts: At the end of a word, y sounds like Spanish i. The examples avoid the separate final ay, ey, oy, and uy patterns.
description: Pronounce final y like “ee” in “see,” not like the English consonant y in “yes.”

example_words.cultural_context: The same sport as in English
The same distilled drink as in English

thoughts: Final ay is a single gliding vowel sound, not two separate syllables.
description: Pronounce it like “eye” in English: start with an open “ah” sound and glide toward “ee.”

example_words.cultural_context: South American country with the same name in English
A mild exclamation you may hear in conversation

thoughts: At the end of a word, ey represents an e sound gliding into an ee-like sound. English speakers know a similar sound from “say.”
description: Pronounce ey like the vowel sound in English “say”: start with a clear “eh” and glide toward “ee.”

thoughts: Word-final oy forms the same familiar diphthong as English “oy.”
description: Pronounce oy like the sound in English “boy”: start with an “oh” sound and glide into “y.”

thoughts: Final uy is a quick glide from Spanish u to an English y sound. English speakers know both sounds, but may need practice joining them smoothly.
description: Say “oo” as in “food,” then glide quickly into “y” as in “yes”: roughly “ooy.” Keep it together rather than pronouncing two separate syllables.

thoughts: The h is silent, and ie forms a glide into the e vowel. At the start of a word, the glide may sound slightly stronger in some Latin American accents.
description: Usually sounds like “yeh”: start with the y sound in “yes,” then say a short, clear “eh.” Do not pronounce the h.

thoughts: The h is silent; the u and e form a single syllable, often with a slight g-like onset in everyday speech.
description: Say “weh,” roughly like the start of English “well,” but without the final l. The h is silent. You may hear a slight g-like sound before “weh,” especially at the beginning of a word.

example_words.cultural_context: An everyday word for a bone

thoughts: The h is silent; the u and i combine into a sound much like English “wee.”
description: Pronounce “hui” like English “wee.” The h is silent, and the u glides quickly into the i.

example_words.cultural_context: Word for an escape or getaway

thoughts: At the end of a word, Spanish d is usually softer than English d and may be barely audible in casual speech.
description: In careful speech, make a soft sound like the th in English “breathe,” with your tongue against your upper teeth. Don’t pronounce it as a strong English d. In casual speech, it may become very faint or disappear.

example_words.cultural_context: Similar to the English word university

thoughts: The ending is pronounced the same way across these examples. The accent marks the stressed vowel, and Latin American Spanish pronounces the c as s.
description: Pronounce it roughly “SYOHN”: an s sound followed by a quick y glide and a stressed “ohn.” Keep the o steady rather than turning it into an English-style “oh-oo.”

thoughts: The ending is one stressed syllable. Unlike the ending of English “vision,” its s has a clear /s/ sound.
description: Say “syohn” as one syllable: an s sound, a quick y sound, then a stressed “ohn.” Keep the s crisp, not like the “zh” in English “vision.”
